article.plain_text:
Prime Editing 是 2019 年由 David Liu 實驗室發表的基因編輯技術。它與傳統 CRISPR-Cas9 以及已成熟的 CAR-T 療法，在機制、適用疾病與臨床成熟度上有明顯不同。本文將三者並列，說明目前各自能做什麼、做不到什麼，以及為什麼它們不是互相取代的工具。
 
一、三種技術在做什麼
CAR-T 是把病人自己的 T 細胞取出，裝上能辨認癌細胞表面標記的嵌合抗原受體（CAR），再擴增後回輸。回輸後的細胞會在體內增殖並攻擊帶有目標抗原的細胞，因此被稱為「活的藥物」。它直接針對癌症，而非修正病人原本的基因錯字。
CRISPR-Cas9 使用 Cas9 酶在引導 RNA 定位後，將雙股 DNA 剪斷，再依賴細胞自身的修復機制。它擅長破壞基因（基因敲除），也可在有模板時做較大片段插入，但精準修正的效率與安全性受雙股斷裂影響。
Prime Editing 使用只剪一股的切口酶加上逆轉錄酶，根據 pegRNA 提供的模板，直接在指定位置寫入新的 DNA 序列。設計上通常不產生雙股斷裂，較適合修正點突變、小插入或小刪除。理論上可處理約 90% 的已知致病突變。
比喻
CAR-T 像派出一支重新訓練的特種部隊去攻擊敵人。CRISPR-Cas9 像用剪刀把電線剪斷，再希望電工能正確接回去。Prime Editing 像用一支能定位的筆，直接改寫說明書上的錯字，不必先把電線剪斷。
 
二、目前主要用於什麼疾病
CAR-T 已是獲批療法，主要用於血液惡性腫瘤：
復發或難治的 B 細胞急性淋巴性白血病
特定類型的大 B 細胞淋巴瘤
套細胞淋巴瘤
多發性骨髓瘤（BCMA 靶點）
自 2017 年首款產品獲 FDA 批准以來，全球已有超過三萬名患者接受治療。實體腫瘤方面，中國已批准首款針對 CLDN18.2 陽性胃癌的產品（Satri-cel），但仍屬適應症很窄的突破。主要障礙包括 T 細胞難以穿透腫瘤、腫瘤微環境抑制、缺乏理想單一靶點，以及細胞容易耗竭。
Prime Editing 目前仍處早期臨床，重點在單基因疾病而非癌症：
慢性肉芽腫病（CGD）：體外編輯（PM359），已有正面臨床數據，並獲 RMAT 認定
威爾遜氏症：體內編輯（PM577a），2026 年 10 月已完成首例給藥，初步數據預計 2027 年
α1-抗胰蛋白酶缺乏症（AATD）：已獲美國 IND（PM647）
目前沒有針對癌症的 Prime Editing 臨床項目。研究上有人用它模擬癌細胞突變或改良 T 細胞療法的可控性，但這些尚未進入治療癌症的臨床階段。
CRISPR-Cas9 已有多項臨床應用與獲批產品，涵蓋基因敲除型細胞療法與部分體內編輯項目。它在需要「關掉」致病基因的場景較成熟。
 
 
三、機制與安全性差異

 
CAR-T 的毒性（細胞因子釋放症候群、神經毒性）需要在有經驗的中心處理。Prime Editing 理論上因避免雙股斷裂而降低某些風險，但長期安全性與遞送效率仍在驗證。
四、製程差異
CAR-T 主流仍是自體體外製造：抽血 → 分離 T 細胞 → 基因改造 → 擴增 → 回輸。過程耗時且昂貴。異體現貨與體內製造是發展方向，但尚未成為主流。
Prime Editing 同時有體外路線（如 CGD）與體內 LNP 路線（如威爾遜氏症）。體內路線目標是一次靜脈注射，省去抽細胞送廠的步驟，但目前仍屬早期驗證。
五、未來可能的交會點
研究顯示，Prime Editing 可被用來改良 T 細胞療法。例如，有團隊用它在 T 細胞上同時做基因修正與引入藥物抗性，讓細胞在使用免疫抑制劑時仍能存活並可被藥物控制。這有助於提高 CAR-T 的安全性與可控性，但仍屬研究階段。
另外，Prime Editing 的延伸技術（如 PASSIGE）也被探索用於較大片段的定點插入，理論上可用於更精準地製造 CAR-T 細胞，減少隨機插入帶來的品質差異。
六、總結
CAR-T 是已落地的癌症免疫細胞療法，在血液腫瘤有真實成果與患者規模，實體腫瘤仍在突破。
CRISPR-Cas9 是成熟的基因編輯工具，擅長基因破壞，已有多項臨床應用。
Prime Editing 是更早期的「搜尋並取代」平台，目前在單基因疾病驗證精準修正是否可行，尚未直接用於癌症治療。
三者不是互相取代，而是不同工具。CAR-T 解決「如何讓免疫細胞攻擊癌細胞」，CRISPR-Cas9 解決「如何有效破壞基因」，Prime Editing 則嘗試「如何精準改對錯字」。未來若在細胞製造精準度上結合，可能產生新的應用空間，但
目前成熟度與應用範圍差異明顯。
 
 
本文僅整理公開科學機制與現況，不構成醫療或投資建議。

What if immunosuppressive drugs could become tools to control therapeutic T cells rather than simply suppress them?

A major challenge in cell and gene therapy is the lack of clinically practical ways to selectively expand or eliminate engineered cells inside the body. This becomes particularly important when patients cannot discontinue immunosuppression, such as transplant recipients or individuals with immune dysregulation.

A new study introduces a multiplex prime-editing platform that turns commonly used immunosuppressive drugs into pathway-specific switches for controlling therapeutic T cells in vivo.

The investigators demonstrated several important applications:

Correcting pathogenic mutations: Prime editing corrected multiple immune dysregulation-associated variants in primary human T cells, including the HAVCR2 driver mutation in cells from patients with subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (SPTCL).

Selective expansion: Combining gene correction with drug-resistance editing enabled corrected SPTCL T cells to expand selectively under immunosuppressive pressure in humanized mouse models.

Reversible control: These engineered cells retained sensitivity to alternative agents, providing a potential mechanism for rapid in vivo suppression.

Broader applicability: Drug-resistant antigen-specific and CAR T cells maintained effector function despite pharmacologic immunosuppression.

Importantly, genomic, transcriptional, immunophenotypic, and clonal analyses demonstrated minimal off-target perturbation in the studied systems.

The implications extend beyond correcting inherited or acquired immune dysfunction. This strategy could help make CAR-T and other cellular therapies compatible with clinical settings in which immunosuppression is unavoidable.

The conceptual shift is significant: instead of asking patients to stop immunosuppression to protect therapeutic cells, we may be able to engineer therapeutic cells to function within—and be selectively controlled by—that immunosuppressive environment.

These remain preclinical findings, but they introduce a compelling framework for more controllable, adaptable cell therapies.

自CRISPR问世以来，人类基因组编辑始终被困在一种“剪刀与胶水”的被动隐喻中。Cas9等核酸酶本质上只是可编程的分子剪刀：它们负责切断双链DNA，而后续的修复、敲除或外源片段插入，则完全听凭宿主细胞自身的修复机制（NHEJ或HDR）摆布。在成年神经元、心肌细胞及造血干细胞等非分裂细胞中，同源重组修复（HDR）几乎彻底休眠；依靠双链断裂诱导大片段治疗性基因插入不仅效率极低，更伴随着随机插入突变、染色体大片段缺失与p53介导的细胞凋亡等巨大毒性风险。碱基编辑与先导编辑（Prime Editing）虽避免了双链断裂，却受限于载荷容量，难以将跨越数千乃至上万碱基的完整功能基因精准搬运到位。而传统的位点特异性重组酶（如Cre或Bxb1）虽能在不释放游离断裂的前提下搬运超大载荷，却被锁死在固定的天然识别位点（如loxP）上，缺乏任何RNA引导的可编程性。

彻底打破这一鸿沟的划时代里程碑，来自Arc Institute（阿克研究所）Patrick Hsu、Silvana Konermann团队与东京大学Hiroshi Nishimasu等科学家携手揭示的自然奇迹：桥连RNA（Bridge RNA）系统。
研究团队在对古老细菌转座子IS110家族的系统性探寻中，发现了前所未见的生命底层机制。IS110重组酶并不直接以蛋白质刚性识别DNA靶标，而是装配了一条具有双内环结构的高级非编码RNA——“桥连RNA”。该RNA通过两个完全独立、各自可编程的结合环分别行使导航功能：
一个环（Target-binding loop）通过碱基互补精准锚定基因组上的目标位点；
另一个环（Donor-binding loop）则同等精准地特异性钳夹待插入的供体DNA片段。

这一双环架构赋予了重组酶超乎想象的工程自由度。研究人员只需按需设计两个RNA环的核苷酸序列，即可同时定义“剪切位点”与“粘合载荷”。在反应过程中，IS110重组酶协同执行四条DNA链的协同断裂与互换再连接，在完全不释放游离双链DNA断裂、完全不依赖宿主细胞DNA修复酶系的前提下，完成了从基因插入、大片段反转（Inversion）到大片段精准切除（Excision）的一体化拓扑重组。在生化与细胞验证中，该系统对千碱基级供体分子的定点插入特异性高达94%以上，重组效率突破60%，且由于无需依赖宿主修复途径，其在大片段基因操控中展现出跨细胞周期的普遍适用性。

从CRISPR单纯的“剪切-修补”拼图，跃升至由桥连RNA主导的“原位重组与文本替换”，Bridge RNA不仅填补了RNA可编程性与兆碱基级重组酶之间的世纪空白，更将生命科学推向了真正的基因组全景文字处理时代：在不伤及基因组完整性的宁静中，整段缺失的治疗性基因与合成生物学电路，终于拥有了自由起落的精准着陆场。

Why is $NVDA so significant? It serves as the primary demand anchor for the entire AI hardware supply chain. Any shift in its orders or guidance triggers a ripple effect, forcing a recalibration of production schedules and capacity expansion plans across the ecosystem. When Nvidia "coughs," the rest of the chain often "catches a cold"—though this isn't an absolute rule.

In the last quarter, Nvidia’s data center revenue reached $88.9 billion, with guidance for the upcoming quarter hovering around $108 billion. Jensen Huang noted earlier this year that Nvidia has become TSMC’s largest customer. An AI server is far more than just a GPU; it requires a full suite of components—memory, advanced packaging, optical and electrical interconnects, and cooling systems. The initial orders for many of these components are driven directly by Nvidia’s shipment cadence.

Consequently, Nvidia occupies a unique position. Cloud service providers require computing power, which leads them to place orders with Nvidia; these orders are then broken down into requirements for memory, packaging, optics, electronics, and cooling. Any company integrated into this supply chain is, therefore, highly sensitive to Nvidia’s guidance.

Let’s trace the chain. In the memory sector, HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is integrated directly into Nvidia’s GPUs—with the upcoming "Rubin" generation utilizing HBM4. During an earnings call this August, Nvidia’s CFO confirmed that the company is collaborating with Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron ($MU) to expand capacity. Advanced process nodes and CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) packaging are primarily handled by TSMC ($TSM). In optical communications, Nvidia is pushing its own Spectrum-X and Quantum-X platforms, which feature co-packaged optics; the company has stated that the Spectrum-X line has already entered production. Public disclosures indicate that companies such as Coherent ($COHR), Lumentum, Finisar ($FN), Zhongji Innolight, and Eoptolink are part of this ecosystem. For Finisar ($FN), Nvidia accounted for 16% of its revenue in the most recent fiscal year. Lumentum, meanwhile, announced this month that it is set to be acquired by Marvell ($MRVL), though the deal has yet to close. In the networking space, the ecosystem includes both Nvidia’s own Spectrum-X and products from Arista Networks ($ANET). Broadcom ($AVGO) plays a dual role: it supplies components for custom chips—such as Google’s TPUs—while also producing switching chips, making it both a partner in the supply chain and a competitor to Nvidia. Further upstream, demand for equipment from Applied Materials ($AMAT), Lam Research ($LRCX), and ASML ($ASML) is largely driven by the capacity expansion efforts of TSMC and HBM manufacturers. On the server front, companies like Dell ($DELL), Supermicro ($SMCI), and Foxconn (Hon Hai) are actively developing systems based on the "Vera Rubin" architecture. Meanwhile, Vertiv ($VRT) is collaborating with them to provide 800V high-voltage DC power and liquid cooling solutions.

The events of November 5th illustrate this most clearly: when Nvidia ($NVDA) fell 9.3%, the aforementioned stocks all tumbled—many even more sharply. Micron ($MU) dropped 17%, while Vertiv ($VRT), Applied Materials ($AMAT), Finisar/Coherent ($FN/COHR), and Lam Research ($LRCX) all saw double-digit declines. Over the past 251 trading days, there were 28 instances where Nvidia fell by more than 3% in a single day; on 22 of those days, stocks across the memory, optical module, TSMC, networking, power, and semiconductor equipment sectors also fell. In terms of daily price correlation, TSMC ($TSM) shows the strongest link at approximately 0.67; Coherent ($COHR) and Vertiv ($VRT) sit around 0.51; Micron ($MU) and Applied Materials ($AMAT) are near 0.48; and Arista Networks ($ANET) is around 0.44. This represents a moderate-to-strong correlation—not a perfect 1.0—meaning that while these stocks tend to move in tandem, the magnitude and timing of their fluctuations can vary.

Yet, on November 9th, when Nvidia fell 4.3%, sectors like memory, optical modules, and semiconductor equipment actually rebounded. Demand isn't solely dependent on Nvidia; for instance, custom ASICs—such as Google’s TPU—also drive demand for advanced packaging, HBM (High Bandwidth Memory), and optical modules, with Broadcom ($AVGO) playing a key role in that ecosystem.

Understanding this supply chain is essential to grasping Nvidia’s true position. My advice: if you’re going to invest, do it in batches. Avoid leverage, don’t chase highs, and remember—being bullish doesn’t mean you have to stubbornly hold on no matter what.

A critical reminder from semiconductor physicist Dr. Maksym Plakhotnyuk on advanced packaging bottlenecks: cleanroom capacity reflects atomic process control rather than floor space.

Sell-side models assume building cleanrooms linearly doubles CoWoS and HBM output. Physical reality on the fab floor operates under three harsh yield constraints:

Sub-Nanometer Thin Film Uniformity: In 16-high HBM4 and CoWoS-L, inter-die dielectric layers thin down to single microns. Nanometer-level ALD thickness variances cause catastrophic dielectric breakdown under thermal cycling.

CMP Planarization Limits: Direct copper-to-copper hybrid bonding mandates surface roughness below 0.5nm. CMP dishing of a single nanometer creates interface micro-voids and open circuits that destroy compound packaging yield.

Thermal Warpage and CTE Mismatch: A 6x coefficient of thermal expansion mismatch between silicon interposers (2.6 ppm/°C) and organic ABF substrates (16 ppm/°C) causes severe die warpage during thermal compression bonding.

Advanced packaging capacity cannot be bought with CapEx alone. Yield is governed by process physics, maintaining structural supply tightness across 2027.

英伟达从不自己建厂所以芯片能出多少货很大程度上取决于台积电给多少产能。
 
2. 真正的瓶颈先进封装 CoWoS
AI 芯片要把 GPU 裸片和多颗 HBM 显存封装在一起这一步叫 CoWoS近年一直是整条供应链最紧的环节比晶圆制造本身更紧。

台积电计划到 2026 年底把 CoWoS 月产能提升到约 15 万片较 2024 年底增长近四倍。
包装复杂度还在上升Rubin 采用更大的封装面积对良率和基板提出更高要求。有报道称 Rubin Ultra 原本传闻要集成四颗 GPU 裸片最终因封装限制改为两颗。

Blackwell 用定制的 4nm 级工艺N4P
Rubin 计划采用台积电 N3P3nm并搭配 HBM4。
TrendForce 估计 AI 在台积电 3nm 产能中的占比将从 2025 年的 5% 升至 2026 年的 36%。
 
每代新品几乎都用台积电当时最先进或次先进的节点双方路线图高度同步。
 
3. 英伟达为什么要包下产能
挤压对手产能被锁定后AMD 和云厂商自研芯片能拿到的封装资源更少
保证交付AI 需求远超供给谁有产能谁拿订单
形成壁垒这被一些分析称为算力护城河除了 CUDA供应链锁定也是护城河
 
不过要注意具体分配比例来自分析师和供应链报道台积电不公开按客户披露。

地缘政治先进制程和封装高度集中在台湾两岸局势是最大的尾部风险

周期风险若 AI 需求放缓英伟达可能砍单台积电的 AI 产能扩张会面临库存和利用率压力

英伟达的出货上限 约等于 台积电 CoWoS 产能 乘以 良率 乘以 HBM 供应

前回の#1-2で、AIチップは誰が設計してもTSMCの工場へ行くと書いた。しかし工場でチップを作ったら終わりではない。AIチップ1つは、計算するチップとHBM（広帯域メモリ）を何個も1つの体につなげて初めて完成する。このつなげる工程がパッケージングで、2024年からAIチップの供給をいちばん強く止めていたマスがまさにここだった。チップは作り終えていたのに、つなげる場所がなくて出荷できなかったのだ。
パッケージングとは何か
昔のパッケージングは、完成したチップをプラスチックで包んで足をつける後仕上げの作業だった。技術より人件費の勝負なので、台湾や東南アジアに出ていった工程だ。AIチップは違う。エヌビディアのGPUは計算チップの横にHBMを8個ずつつなげるが、これらのチップは毎秒数テラバイトをやり取りしなければならないので、とても細かい道でつなぐ必要がある。TSMCはシリコンの板（インターポーザー）の上にチップとメモリを並べて載せ、それをさらに基板に載せる方式を使っていて、これがCoWoSだ。シリコンの板を作ること自体が半導体工程なので、どこでもできるわけではない。
どれだけ詰まっていたか
TSMCのCoWoS生産能力は、2023年末の月1万3,000〜1万6,000枚から、2024年末に3万5,000〜4万枚、2025年末に6万5,000〜7万5,000枚と、毎年2倍近く増えた。2026年末には機関の推計で月12万〜14万枚だ。TSMC自身、2022年から2027年まで毎年80%を超えて増やすと言った。それでも足りない。2026年は需要に対して供給が約20%不足するという推計が出ていて、TSMCの魏哲家会長は2026年7月の決算発表で、パッケージングの能力がぎりぎりすぎて顧客の成長を妨げていると直接述べた。
エヌビディアが2026年のTSMC CoWoSの数量の半分以上にあたる80万〜85万枚を先に押さえたことも大きかった。そのうえ次のチップであるルービンはチップが大きくなり、ウェハー1枚から取れるチップが9個ほどに減る。チップが大きくなるほど、同じ工場から出てくる数が減る構造だ。
あふれた注文はどこへ行くのか
TSMCはもともと、シリコンの板にチップをつなげる前工程は自社で行い、基板に載せる後工程だけを外注していた。2026年8月の報道では、前工程まで外注を広げることにした。この数量をいちばん多く受け取るのが、世界最大のパッケージング会社である台湾のASEだ。
ASEは2026年第3四半期の売上が2,441億台湾ドルで1年前より44.8%増え、営業利益率は13.6%だった。最先端パッケージング（LEAP）の売上見通しを2026年に40億ドル以上へ引き上げ、2027年はその2倍を見込んでいる。2026年の設備投資を過去最大の105億ドルに引き上げたが、それでも需要が供給を上回ると述べた。
米国のアムコーは2026年第3四半期の売上が19億9,100万ドルで、1年前とほぼ同じだった。営業利益率は8.0%から11.3%に上がったが、時価総額は約92億ドルと小さい。TSMCと10年の長期契約を結び、アリゾナにパッケージング工場を建設中だが、生産は2028年初めからだ。
インテルは別の道を掘っている。EMIB-Tという自社のパッケージングをCoWoSの代わりとして売り込んでいる。チップあたりのコストが数百ドルで、CoWoSの900〜1,000ドルより安いという分析があり、グーグルが次のTPUに使うという報道も出た。ただしインテル・ファウンドリーの外部売上は2026年第2四半期に2億9,300万ドルしかなく、まだ契約が数字に表れたものはない。
装置の側ではオランダのBESIがある。チップとチップをはんだなしで直接つなげるハイブリッドボンディング装置を作っていて、第3四半期の売上は1年前より113.6%、受注は96.1%増えた。次世代のHBMとチップの積み重ねにこの装置が入る。
いつ解消するのか
パッケージングは、生産より早く解消するマスだ。最先端の生産は工場を建てるのに何年もかかり、装置もASML1社に並ばなければならないが、パッケージングはTSMCが古い8インチ工場を改造しても増やせるし、ASE、アムコー、インテルが一緒に増やす。台湾の報道では、TSMCのCoWoSは2028年末に月26万枚と2026年末の2倍になり、トレンドフォースは2027年から不足が解消し始めると見ている。その次の技術は、丸いウェハーの代わりに四角い板を使うパネルパッケージングで、TSMCは2028〜2029年の量産、ASEは2027年第1四半期の量産を目標にしている。
結論
パッケージングは2024〜2026年のAIチップのボトルネックの主役だったが、チップのマスの中ではいちばん先に解消すると考える。生産はTSMCが1社で握っているので解消しないが、パッケージングは複数の会社が一緒に増やせるマスだからだ。だから、このマスでお金を稼ぐ場所は、ボトルネックを握る側ではなく、あふれた数量を受け取る側だ。TSMCが受け切れなかった数量はASEへ行っていて、ASEの利益率も一緒に上がっている。パッケージングのマスでいちばん確かな場所はASEだと考える。アムコーは米国工場が2028年にようやく動き出し、利益率も低いので一歩遅れていて、インテルは契約が数字に表れるまでは期待の段階だ。
次回は、これらすべての工場を埋める機械、#1-4装置だ。

中国为何造不出Blackwell芯片？主要是制造这一环被卡住了，不是芯片设计不行。顺带一提，英伟达自己也不造芯片，Blackwell 是台积电代工的。
光刻机：Blackwell 用的是台积电 4 纳米级工艺，量产要靠 ASML 的极紫外光刻机（EUV）。荷兰和美国的出口管制让中国买不到。中芯国际只能用上一代深紫外光刻机（DUV）反复曝光，能做到 7 纳米，勉强摸到 5 纳米级，但良率低、成本高、产能有限。
高带宽内存（HBM）：每颗 Blackwell 旁边要配好几颗 HBM3E。这种内存基本由 SK 海力士、三星、美光三家供应，也在管制范围内。国产 HBM 还在追赶，落后一到两代。
先进封装：Blackwell 把两颗大芯片和多颗 HBM 封装在一起，用的是台积电的 CoWoS-L 封装技术。国内封装厂在做类似技术，但规模和成熟度还差一截。
设备和软件链：刻蚀、沉积、量测设备，芯片设计软件（EDA）和一部分现成的电路设计模块（IP 核），也受美国管制。国产替代在推进，但还不齐全。
软件生态：就算硬件做出来，英伟达还有积累多年的 CUDA 软件和大批开发者，这块比硬件更难追。
现状是国内能做出可用的 AI 芯片，比如华为昇腾，但单颗的性能、能效和产量都比 Blackwell 低一档，只能靠多堆芯片、搭大集群来弥补。

Introduction
Weaker consumer electronics demand is unlikely to relieve foundry shortages: We expect advanced-node supply to remain tight through 2027, with AI-linked mature and specialty processes constrained through at least the first half of the year.
TSMC’s third-quarter results show AI demand continuing to lift the foundry outlook even as consumer markets lose momentum. GPUs and AI ASICs remain important, but the sources of growth are broadening: server CPUs and HBM logic base dies add demand for advanced nodes, while power management, optical communications, analog chips and silicon interposers support mature processes.
Q3 2026 Review: Strong AI Demand Offsets a Subdued Consumer Peak Season
Foundry revenue continued to expand in the third quarter:
TSMC: up 17.6% quarter over quarter and approximately 51% year over year.
United Microelectronics: up 8% sequentially and 25.6% year over year.
Vanguard International Semiconductor, a specialty foundry: up 10.2% sequentially and 27.2% year over year.
Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing: up 23.4% sequentially and 80.3% year over year.
The broad improvement across end markets in the first half has given way to a clearer divergence between AI and consumer demand:
TSMC’s high-performance computing revenue grew 82.7% year over year in Q3, faster than the 46% growth recorded in the first half.
Smartphone revenue grew just 4.3% year over year, slowing from 19.1% in the first half.
Its Digital Consumer Electronics platform declined for a second consecutive quarter.
HPC includes more than AI, but the contrast with consumer-facing platforms is clear.
Since late 2025, phone and PC makers have brought some chip purchases forward to get ahead of rising memory and processor prices. That supported consumer-chip orders and the processes serving them in the first half of 2026.
Purchases brought forward also borrow from future demand.
With memory and processor prices continuing to rise, I expect that earlier buying to become harder to sustain in the second half. This is my interpretation of the stronger AI demand and weaker consumer momentum visible in TSMC’s Q3 business.
The pattern is consistent with the view we have maintained over the past three quarters:
Consumer logic ICs: purchases brought forward are unlikely to last, and visibility into the second half of 2026 is limited.
Advanced Nodes: Strong 2nm, 3nm and 5nm Demand Keeps Supply Tight Through 2027
Weaker non-AI demand is unlikely to free enough capacity to resolve shortages in advanced logic. We continue to expect tight supply across 2nm, 3nm, 5nm and advanced packaging through 2027.
Strong GPU, ASIC and CPU Demand Expands Requirements for 2nm, 3nm and 5nm
GPUs and AI ASICs handle the bulk of AI training and inference computation. Their use of TSMC’s 3nm and 5nm technologies has supported rapid demand growth since 2024.
Agentic AI adds substantial work around that computation: calling tools, querying internal retrieval-augmented generation databases, searching the web, and writing and retrieving intermediate data.
CPUs are well suited to many of these control, data movement and storage tasks, adding another source of server-processor demand.
At the time of the October report, AMD had projected server CPU revenue growth above 80% year over year in the second half of 2026 and above 70% in 2027. Its Turin platform uses TSMC’s 3nm and 5nm processes, while Venice moves to 2nm. Demand for both generations expands requirements across those nodes.
Intel has also pointed to strong double-digit server CPU unit growth in 2026, with momentum extending into 2027. Sapphire Rapids and Emerald Rapids use Intel 7, while Granite Rapids and Sierra Forest compute tiles use Intel 3. Strong demand increases the need for capacity on Intel’s own processes as well.
GPU and ASIC demand is therefore being joined by an additional CPU requirement.
We expect this combination to keep advanced manufacturing capacity under pressure in 2027.
 
HBM Base Dies Move Toward 3nm and 4nm, Extending Demand Into 2028 and Beyond
HBM combines multiple stacked DRAM dies with a logic base die. The DRAM stores data; the base die handles connections, data movement, signaling and control.
 
Higher bandwidth, tighter power budgets and more complex logic are pushing the base die toward advanced logic processes. HBM4 already includes designs using TSMC’s 12nm technology and Samsung’s in-house 4nm process.
The next stage of adoption can create another meaningful market for advanced foundry capacity.
Our estimates in the October report were:
NVIDIA alone could require approximately 27,000 12-inch base-die wafers per month in 2027, rising to 38,000–39,000 in 2028.
TSMC’s 3nm capacity could reach approximately 190,000–205,000 wafers per month in 2027.
The NVIDIA figures cover total base-die requirements across processes. The portion moving to 3nm depends on the adoption schedule.
Under our phased-adoption scenario for NVIDIA-related base dies, this application could represent approximately 3% of TSMC’s 3nm demand in 2028 and 10% in 2029.
This changes how we view the life of an advanced node. In earlier transitions, growth at a previous-generation node often slowed as customers moved to the newest process. HBM base dies create a new application that can support 3nm even as leading compute products move to 2nm.
The opportunity also depends on the customer. NVIDIA’s reported preference for TSMC 3nm in custom NVHBM could move base-die manufacturing outside Samsung Foundry, even when Samsung remains the HBM supplier. Other GPU and ASIC customers could choose differently. If Samsung’s own process meets their requirements, it could retain that manufacturing work within the group.
GPU, ASIC, CPU and HBM base-die demand are adding to advanced-node requirements at the same time. TSMC raised its 2026 revenue growth outlook to approximately 44% in US dollar terms, compared with an outlook above 30% earlier in the year.
This is consistent with our view over the past three quarters:
With AI demand continuing to be revised upward, we estimate that advanced-node foundry production value could grow 30–40% or more in 2026.
We also maintain our earlier view:
Advanced-node supply shortages will persist through the second half of 2026 and into 2027.
Mature Nodes: Server Power, Optical, Analog and Silicon Interposer Demand Keeps Supply Tight Through H1 2027
Building a new fab takes years, so new construction cannot immediately resolve advanced-node shortages. Our research indicates that TSMC and Samsung have been reallocating some space previously used for mature processes toward advanced manufacturing since the first half of 2026, reducing the capacity available for mature-node products.
Mature processes are now supported by both tighter supply and rising AI infrastructure demand.
Inference and agentic AI require more servers, increasing demand for the power-management, optical communications and analog chips around the main processors.
The October report identified several examples:
Vanguard: AI server power-management demand is growing strongly. The company is shifting some display-driver capacity toward higher-end power-management ICs. As mentioned in our previous article, demand still exceeds the supply available after that shift. The conversion involves process upgrades; spare capacity on an older process is not automatically a substitute for a fully loaded finer-geometry line.
Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation: strong AI server demand is supporting power-management requirements, with the report citing order visibility extending to the end of 2027.
GlobalFoundries : the report cited an increase in its 2026 data-center growth outlook from 37–39% to 50–60%, led by silicon photonics, which was expected to more than double and account for roughly 40% of that business.
Infineon, Texas Instruments and Analog Devices: their AI power, data-center power and optical communications businesses provide further evidence that demand extends beyond the main compute chips.
AI demand can therefore absorb capacity released by weaker consumer display-driver demand, while some of the relevant processes remain constrained.
Silicon interposers for CoWoS-S add another source of mature-node demand.
Although CoWoS is advanced packaging, its silicon interposer can use mature logic processes such as 65nm. Strong packaging demand thus increases requirements for mature wafer manufacturing as well.
TSMC has been expanding external support for this work:
UMC’s roadmap in the report called for interposer tape-out around late 2026 to early 2027, with a more meaningful revenue contribution during 2027.
GlobalFoundries announced an approximately US$2 billion, five-year agreement with TSMC in October 2026 to manufacture silicon interposers for advanced packaging, with a production ramp planned for the first half of 2028.
The GlobalFoundries capacity arrives later than the near-term shortage window. It illustrates the expansion underway rather than an immediate source of supply relief.
With mature-node supply being reallocated and AI infrastructure expanding, we maintain the view we have held since mid-June 2026:
Mature-node logic supply and demand should be stronger than expected in the second half. Production value for 8-inch and 12-inch mature processes should benefit from steadily rising volumes and prices.
We expect tight supply in AI-linked mature and specialty processes to continue through at least the first half of 2027.

2️⃣ ASML 제재 속 'DUV 4중 노광(SAQP)'의 치명적 기술 한계

• 구형 DUV 장비로 웨이퍼를 4번 겹쳐 굽는 사중 패터닝(SAQP)을 강행했으나, 나노미터 단위의 레이어 오정렬(Overlay Error)과 발열 결함 속출
• 수율을 끌어올릴 물리적 장비가 없어, 2026년까지 화웨이 AI 칩 공정이 구형 7나노 레벨에 강제로 묶여버리는 병목 발생

3️⃣ 바이트댄스·알리바바의 불만과 암시장 H100 밀수 폭증
• 바이트댄스(틱톡 모회사)가 올해 주문한 어센드 910B/C 10만 개 중 실제 납품된 물량은 3만 개 미만으로 극심한 공급 차질

If you've talked to anyone about AI hardware this year, you've heard it. HBM is the bottleneck.

I agree. But when I went through Micron's latest segment numbers, one line stopped me. The business unit that holds HBM ran an 83% gross margin, and that was the lowest of Micron's four units. The fattest margins, 90%, sat in the units that mostly sell conventional DRAM and NAND, the stuff HBM is crowding out of the fab. Micron's CFO said that unit's margin was flat because higher pricing was offset by more HBM in the mix.

So I want to ask a different question here. How profitable HBM is matters 
less than you'd think. What matters is how many front-end wafers and how 
much cleanroom space HBM is eating, and whose P&L that bill finally lands 
on.
 

My read is HBM stays scarce through 2027. But the money mostly lands in conventional DRAM pricing and in memory makers' cash flow, not in HBM gross margin. That's a call, not a conclusion, so below I've laid out what's reported, what I calculated, where I'm interpreting, and what would make me wrong.

Quick key. Reported means the company or a named source said it. C
alculated means I did the arithmetic from public numbers. My read means 
it's my interpretation.
 



2 · The story the market's already telling

The consensus story is pretty simple. AI accelerators keep getting bigger, each one carries more HBM, and all three memory makers win on volume and price.

Reported.
- Micron says industry DRAM bit supply grows in the mid 20s percent in 2026 and the low 20s in 2027 and 2028, supply constrained both years. Its phrase for when supply and demand balance out is no line of sight.
- Micron says it's wrapped up agreements for most of its 2027 HBM bits, at sharply higher prices year over year.
- Samsung's 3Q26 operating profit came in at KRW 107.4tn, a record and in line with consensus.
- Jensen Huang said in June that all three memory makers had qualified HBM4 for Vera Rubin and all three were in production.

Most of that is already in the stock prices. I'm more interested in three things that get talked about a lot less.

3 · What the market's skipping

First, HBM isn't as profitable as people assume. Micron itself describes HBM price increases as closing the margin gap with conventional DRAM. Read that again. It means HBM has been the lower margin product. The bigger HBM gets in the mix, the more it can actually dilute a memory maker's blended margin.

Second, what HBM really competes for is front-end capacity. The core of every HBM stack is front-end DRAM die, made on the same advanced node wafers in the same cleanrooms as regular DRAM. Every extra bit of HBM means fewer bits for PCs and phones. You'll hear people say a bit of HBM eats about three times the wafer of DDR5. I couldn't find a company figure or a dated research source for that, so I only use it as an assumption.

Third, the knock-on effects are milder than the headlines and they're splitting. Conventional DRAM contract prices are still rising but the increases are shrinking every quarter. And OEMs aren't all getting hit the same way. My read is commercial-heavy names can pass cost through, and consumer-heavy names get squeezed on both units and margin.

4 · The physical chain

Reported.
- An AI accelerator carries 8 to 12 HBM stacks. Microsoft's Maia 300 uses 8 HBM4 stacks, per trade press.
- A stack is front-end DRAM core die plus a base die, stacked with TSVs and tested, then it goes into TSMC CoWoS and gets packaged next to the GPU.
- Any layer can jam. Here's how I'd rank them.

5 · Where it actually binds

My ranking, strongest evidence first. The facts in each line are reported. The ranking itself is my read.

1. Front-end DRAM wafers and cleanroom space. This is the hardest constraint and the companies say it themselves. Micron says expansion needs new cleanrooms and its FY27 capex step-up goes mostly into buildings. SK Hynix has said its Yongin phase 1 cleanroom opens in early 2027 and that's when real expansion starts. You build cleanrooms in years, not quarters, so I don't see broad relief before 2027.

2. CoWoS packaging could be a second constraint, and TSMC has said as much itself. On its July call C.C. Wei said packaging capacity was so tight it was limiting customers' growth. By the October call he called it a little bit of shortage on the back end and pointed to a GlobalFoundries deal for extra back-end supply. If that tightness lasts, it gates the whole accelerator, and finished HBM waits in line for packaging. I rank it below front-end wafers because TSMC's packaging wording softened between July and October. That's about packaging only. In October Wei also said overall demand is still well above what TSMC can supply.

3. Stack height and yield. SK Hynix said HBM4 entered volume production for major customers in 2Q with yields close to the mature prior generation. 12-high is shipping, 16-high is still in qualification, and 20-high and above needs hybrid bonding. Nobody has named a 16-high customer yet. That's next generation's bottleneck, not today's.

4. Bonding tools are not short right now. Hanmi and Hanwha both won HBM4 bonder orders, and Hanmi's follow-on order pace has actually slowed. Hybrid bonding at scale looks like a post-2028 story. Everything at the tool layer points the same way. There are enough tools. What's short is front-end capacity and next-gen yield.

5. Base die and TSV. I haven't seen evidence of a jam here. If the HBM4E 
base die moves to a 3nm-class node it'll compete with GPUs for the same 
leading-edge capacity, and that could become a new constraint. I can't size it yet.
 

6 · Who has pricing power

Share first. Every share number I can find comes from a single third-party source, and they don't measure the same thing. One is total HBM revenue share in 2Q, roughly half for SK Hynix, about a third for Samsung, under a fifth for Micron. The other is HBM4 shipment share on Rubin, where SK Hynix is estimated at 60 to 70%. Different things being counted, so I won't use them to say share is moving in any direction.

Now price. Reported.
- Micron has closed most of its 2027 HBM contracts at sharply higher prices. Customers put down $12.747bn of cash deposits over the fiscal year, and noncurrent customer contract liabilities went from $0.568bn at the end of May to $12.895bn in early September. Buyers are putting real cash down to lock supply.
- SK Hynix now has long-term agreements with 14 customers, including global cloud providers. That was around 10 at its 2Q results.
- The head of Microsoft's Maia program has said they'll order up to five years ahead.
- SK Hynix says HBM4 sells at a higher price than the generation before it. One industry tracker estimates the gap at a bit under 2x a stack. That's a single estimate, so I only use it as a direction.

My read. On public numbers, pricing power is moving from buyers to the three memory makers. But long-term deals trade some price upside for certainty, and industry research has flagged that some suppliers' contract price mechanisms make their increases lag the market average.

Wednesday's SK Hynix call put that to the test, and here's what came back. The customer count and the volume commitment both held up. On price, the official structure is a mechanism that generally reflects market conditions inside a price range agreed with each customer. It isn't a fixed multi-year price. So the company with the most long-term deals isn't automatically the one raising prices fastest. And management's own framing is that HBM profitability is catching up to conventional DRAM, which is the opposite of pulling away from it.

One thing I keep reminding myself. HBM price increases are chasing conventional DRAM margins. They aren't leaving them behind.



7 · How it shows up in the numbers

My read on how the squeeze travels. HBM and server DRAM soak up advanced node capacity, PC and phone DRAM supply gets tighter, contract prices rise, and OEMs either raise prices and lose units or eat the margin themselves.

The price link is cooling. Reported, from industry research. Conventional DRAM contract prices rose 93 to 98% quarter on quarter in 1Q26 and 58 to 63% in 2Q26, with forecasts of 13 to 18% for 3Q26 and 10 to 15% for 4Q26. Still going up, just more slowly each quarter.

The OEM link is splitting. Reported, from the companies' own results.
- $DELL grew client operating profit 42% year on year last quarter, and client margin rose to 7.6% from 6.4%. But Dell guided that margin back to around 6% for the next two quarters and expects a competitive PC market, likely down in units, in the second half.
- $HPQ grew PC revenue 18% while units fell 16%, and PC operating margin was 4.6%, below its own long-term range. HP expects memory and storage to keep rising as a share of its bill of materials, and said it's too early to guide FY27.
- Xiaomi's smartphone gross margin was 8.5% in 2Q26 versus 11.5% a year earlier, on 31.2 million phones shipped, down 26.5% from 42.4 million. Xiaomi put the margin drop mainly down to higher prices for key components, with memory the one it named.

My read. I'm not going to say OEMs are getting crushed across the board. Consumer is under pressure, phones included. Commercial is passing it through.

Now the memory makers themselves. Calculated, from public parameters.
- Micron guided FQ1'27 revenue to $61.5bn. Every 100bp of gross margin on that is about $615m of gross profit in the quarter, roughly $0.53 a share before tax on about 1.15bn diluted shares, or about $0.45 after Micron's guided tax rate of around 15.5%.
- Micron doesn't break out HBM revenue, so I can't size an HBM-specific sensitivity.
- Micron's FY26 net capex was $27.37bn, and inventory rose from $8.57bn at the end of May to $10.37bn in early September. The customer deposits come in through financing cash flow, not adjusted free cash flow, and Micron says they're returned in the back half of each contract once minimum purchases are met, so watch that when you compare across companies.

SK Hynix reported 3Q26 on Wednesday, so this part is no longer a placeholder.

Reported.
- Revenue KRW 104.6tn, operating profit KRW 83.3tn, an operating margin of about 80%.
- Long-term agreements with 14 customers, covering more than half of total 2027 and 2028 production capacity. Typical term is around five years, and some customers are discussing extensions.
- Price generally sits inside an agreed range with a mechanism that tracks market conditions, and there are deposits and fulfillment terms so purchase plans turn into actual orders and shipments. That's a volume commitment plus a price band. It is not a five-year fixed price.
- On the call, management said 2027 HBM volume and price terms with major customers are done, HBM4's higher value is reflected, and the profitability gap between HBM and conventional DRAM should narrow meaningfully. What they did not disclose is whether 2027 HBM contract prices are above or below 2026.
- 2027 capex will be significantly higher than 2026, driven by Yongin phase 1 reaching full operation next year plus other infrastructure. No KRW number, and no split between HBM and conventional DRAM. The last hard number is still the 2Q guide for FY26 capex in the high KRW 40tn range.
- HBM4 overtakes HBM3E in both volume and revenue starting 4Q26. 12-high is shipping on customer schedules. No update on 16-high.
- There's no standalone HBM bit growth number. The company's 2027 view is supply-constrained demand growth in the mid 20s percent for DRAM bits and high teens for NAND. 3Q DRAM bits grew about 10% QoQ and 4Q is guided up in the mid 20s.
- Average DRAM selling price rose in the high 20s percent QoQ in 3Q. Management put that down to firm conventional DRAM prices plus a bigger mix of pricier HBM4.
- Management didn't say what goes into Yongin phase 1 first, HBM or conventional DRAM. What's nailed down is the cleanroom and front-end timing, not the product mix.

Calculated.
- Operating profit beat the LSEG consensus by about KRW 6.6tn (83.3tn versus 76.7tn).
- QoQ, operating profit rose about KRW 22.8tn on about KRW 25.3tn more revenue. That's roughly 0.9 won of extra operating profit per extra won of revenue. My read is that growth was price and mix led. DRAM bits were up only about 10%.

Samsung reported 3Q26 on Thursday morning.

Reported.
- Revenue was KRW 195.3tn and operating profit KRW 107.4tn, in line with the LSEG consensus.
- Samsung's chip division made KRW 106.5tn of operating profit on KRW 147.1tn of revenue, and memory revenue alone was KRW 140.7tn. Samsung says memory profit hit a record, but it didn't give the number.
- On the call, per Korean press coverage, Samsung put its 3Q DRAM price rise at about 20% quarter on quarter and NAND in the high teens. DRAM bit shipments grew only in the low to mid single digits.
- Long-term supply deals are done with 10 large customers, and 10 more are in negotiation. The goal is 60 to 70% of capacity under contract by 2030. There was no update on deposits or price terms.
- HBM4 sales scaled up significantly in 3Q, with no number given. HBM4E mass production starts in the first half of 2027.
- The FY26 capex guide is about KRW 84.4tn, with KRW 76.8tn of it for chips. There's no 2027 figure. Samsung expects AI-driven demand in 2027 to far exceed industry supply, even more so than in 2026.
- Going by Korean press coverage of the call, Samsung gave no 2027 versus 2026 HBM price direction, and neither did SK Hynix. Micron is still the only one of the three to say it out loud.

Calculated.
- The chip division's operating margin was about 72%.

My read. Samsung's quarter looks price-led, just like SK Hynix's. Prices 
went up about a fifth on low single-digit bit growth.




8 · What would prove me wrong

Here's the strongest case against me. We had long-term deals in 2018 and 2022 too, and when prices fell the buyers walked. This round's contracts are mostly price ranges. When Yongin phase 1, Micron's new cleanrooms and CXMT's capacity land in 2027 and 2028, buyers will push prices to the bottom of the range. Add the fact that the extra profit is in conventional DRAM rather than HBM, plus consumer demand already rolling over, and maybe this is just an ordinary shortage. Consumer demand destruction could loosen conventional DRAM well before HBM supply catches up. Industry research itself says long-term deals swap some price upside for a smoother cycle.

I take that seriously. Here's the scorecard after Wednesday, and what would change my mind.

- The SK Hynix test came back without a break. They're at 14 customers, not stuck around 10, and the deals carry a price band with a market mechanism plus deposits. That's more than a volume pledge. The close cousin of that risk is still live though. When supply loosens, buyers could test the floor of the range.
- Any maker's 2027 HBM contract price coming in below 2026. Still live. Micron has said its 2027 HBM prices are sharply higher year on year, but SK Hynix and Samsung gave no direction, so I'm not calling it yet.
- Micron's noncurrent customer contract liabilities flat or down next quarter.
- Micron's HBM to conventional DRAM margin gap widening again.
- Conventional DRAM contract prices falling quarter on quarter in 1H27.
- TSMC saying CoWoS is no longer a constraint while HBM lead times shorten at the same time.
- $AMD holding non-GAAP gross margin at 56% or higher through the MI455 ramp, which would mean memory cost was fully passed through and the idea that buyers absorb some of it is wrong.

So the long-term deal call held, with the range caveat. The 2027 price call is still inconclusive.



9 · What I'm watching next

- Done. SK Hynix 3Q26 on Wednesday. First check came back with deals at 14 customers covering more than half of 2027 and 2028 capacity, price as a range with a market mechanism, and no disclosed 2027 HBM price versus 2026.
- Done. Samsung 3Q26 on Thursday. Operating profit KRW 107.4tn, in line with consensus, memory profit not disclosed, long-term deals at 10 customers with 10 more in talks, and per press coverage of the call no 2027 versus 2026 HBM price direction. Micron remains the only one to give one.
- $AMD in November. Gross margin through the MI455 ramp.
- HP later in November. PC margin and memory share of the bill of materials.
- $MU in December. Noncurrent customer contract liabilities against $12.895bn, and whether the HBM to DRAM margin gap keeps narrowing.
- TSMC's next call in January. Whether packaging is still limiting customers.

My read for now is unchanged. HBM stays scarce through 2027, but the money lands mainly in conventional DRAM pricing and memory makers' cash flow rather than HBM gross margin. If someone prints a 2027 HBM contract price below 2026, if conventional DRAM contract prices turn down, or if TSMC says packaging no longer binds, I'll change my mind. I'll come back with the score after Micron.

Design is one step. The rest is a chain of tools, materials, and process knowledge. That chain is where China’s equipment constraints show up.
One Chip, Several Companies
Take Blackwell B200 as an example. NVIDIA’s design carries 208 billion transistors across two dies. TSMC fabricates it on 4NP, a 4nm-class process. Advanced packaging, CoWoS-L in this case, connects the compute dies and the HBM3E memory that feeds them.
The work splits across three kinds of company. NVIDIA specifies the chip. TSMC builds it. ASML and other equipment suppliers provide the tools that make building possible. A node name like 4nm is a label for a process family, not a dimension you can check with calipers.
Splitting a large design across two dies is one way to keep it manufacturable, and it puts more of the burden on packaging. Fast logic and fast memory only work together if the package can carry the signals between them.
What Lithography Does
A wafer is a thin silicon disc. Fabs build circuits on it one layer at a time, then cut it into dies, the individual pieces that become chips. Lithography is the patterning step. Light transfers a pattern from a mask into a light-sensitive coating. Etch and deposition steps then form the structures that pattern describes.
Two families of lithography tools matter here. Extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, systems pattern some of the most demanding layers in leading-edge processes. ASML is the sole commercial supplier of these systems. Deep ultraviolet, or DUV, tools remain in wide use for other layers and for mature processes.
EUV is not the only route to a small feature. With DUV, finer patterns can require additional patterning, deposition, and etch steps, with tight alignment between them. That extra sequence can raise complexity, extend processing time, and create more opportunities for defects.
This distinction matters when discussing China. Being unable to buy an EUV scanner is a serious constraint. It is not the same as being physically unable to manufacture an advanced chip.
The Chain Behind the Chip
Lithography draws attention, but a fab needs much more.
Deposition equipment lays down thin films. Etch equipment removes material to define structures. Metrology measures what the process actually produced, helping a line catch drift before it ruins a batch. Around those steps sit coating and development, doping and thermal processing, polishing and cleaning, then packaging and testing.
All of it runs inside facilities where contamination control is part of manufacturing, not housekeeping.
Applied Materials, Lam Research, and Tokyo Electron supply major categories of deposition and etch equipment. KLA supplies inspection and metrology systems. ASML supplies lithography. No single company supplies the complete production chain.
Buying the machines also does not transfer the recipes that make them productive. Those recipes specify the chemistry, timing, temperature, tolerances, and sequence that turn equipment into a repeatable process.
The result is measured partly through yield: the proportion of manufactured dies that meet the required specifications. Small losses across many processing steps can accumulate into a large manufacturing problem. A factory can own excellent equipment and still produce too few usable chips.
Can China Buy the Equipment?
There is no single yes-or-no answer for all semiconductor machinery.
Export controls depend on the equipment model, destination, end user, end use, and whether the required license is granted. ASML’s EUV systems have not been supplied to China under the reported licensing restrictions. Some advanced DUV systems and other manufacturing tools face controls as well. Other sales can remain permissible.
That is a selective licensing regime, not a blanket prohibition on equipment sales to China. Permission for one machine, customer, or application does not establish permission for another.
Nor does restricting new purchases make existing manufacturing capability disappear.
SMIC’s 7nm-class chips, including the Kirin 9000S used in Huawei phones in 2023, demonstrate that advanced production is possible without access to ASML EUV systems. What that example does not establish by itself is competitive yield, manufacturing cost, or production volume.
Those are separate questions, and they require separate evidence.
What the Domestic Effort Must Prove
China’s effort to localize semiconductor equipment predates the recent controls, as CSIS has documented. It is therefore too simple to explain the entire effort as a reaction to restrictions, or to treat every subsequent advance as proof that restrictions either worked or failed.
The distinction worth watching is between a prototype and a qualified production line.
A prototype can show that a pattern can be printed or a device can work. A production line must repeat that result across wafers, shifts, maintenance cycles, and batches of materials. It must do so at a usable yield and a sustainable cost.
That is why a report about a domestic lithography machine deserves attention without automatically proving that China has replaced the foreign manufacturing chain. Scanner performance matters. So do reliability, process compatibility, inspection, spare parts, servicing, and the equipment surrounding it.
The same standard applies to any manufacturer claiming a breakthrough. A working device is evidence of capability. Consistent commercial output is evidence of something more.
What a Node Number Leaves Out
For a company trying to compete with NVIDIA, manufacturing a small transistor is only part of the assignment.
Memory and packaging determine how effectively a processor receives data. Power efficiency affects the cost of operating it. Architecture and software determine how much useful work customers can extract from the silicon. Cost per good die belongs on that list, but it is not the whole list.
This is why “Which machine do we need?” is a useful opening question and an incomplete business plan.
The machines are identifiable. The difficult work is making them function together as a production system, then turning that system’s output into a competitive product.
China’s equipment restrictions make parts of that task harder. Domestic advances can reduce particular dependencies. Neither observation settles the larger contest.
The meaningful test is repeatable output: enough good chips, with the right memory and packaging, at a cost and power consumption customers can accept.

11/5那天最直观：$NVDA跌9.3%，上面这些名字全线跟跌，而且不少跌得比它更深，$MU跌了17%，$VRT、$AMAT、$FN、$LRCX也都是两位数。过去一年251个交易日里，它单日跌过3%的日子有28个，存储、光模块、台积电、网络、电源、设备这六只里，有22天是一起跌的。日涨跌相关性，$TSM大约0.67，是最紧的；$COHR、$VRT大约0.51，$MU、$AMAT大约0.48，$ANET大约0.44。相关性中等偏强，到不了1，所以会一起抖，但幅度和节奏可以对不齐。

可11/9它自己跌了4.3%的时候，存储、光模块、设备反而在反弹。谷歌TPU这类ASIC，经由$AVGO同样在吃先进封装、HBM和光模块，需求不全站在它一家身上。

看懂这条链，是为了看清它的位置。兄弟，要做就分批，不上杠杆，不追高，看多不等于死扛。

Ieri sono successe decine di cose sui mercati. Ma se tolgo il rumore, secondo me ce ne sono tre che contano davvero.

Per Nvidia il caso Jensen Huang non è più gossip. È diventato un problema di governance e sicurezza nazionale.

Nel weekend Nvidia $NVDA ha annunciato che il consiglio di amministrazione ha aperto un’indagine indipendente per stabilire se Jensen Huang sia stato il bersaglio di un’operazione di intelligence straniera.

La vicenda nasce da un rapporto secondo cui Huang avrebbe avuto una relazione con Alice Huang, ex dirigente di Megaspeed e nessuna parentela con lui, che secondo quanto riportato dal New York Times sarebbe stata identificata dalle autorità americane come una risorsa dell’intelligence cinese.

Megaspeed è inoltre una società che acquista chip Nvidia $NVDA ed è già stata oggetto di scrutinio negli Stati Uniti per il possibile ruolo nell’accesso cinese a processori AI soggetti ai controlli sulle esportazioni.

Huang nel weekend ha ammesso pubblicamente di essere stato infedele alla moglie e ha detto che collaborerà completamente con l’indagine.

La parte importante per l’investitore, però, non riguarda la sua vita privata.

Riguarda ciò che l’indagine dovrà stabilire.

Il board di Nvidia $NVDA dice al momento di non avere motivo di credere che segreti aziendali o sicurezza nazionale americana siano stati compromessi. Ma il fatto che un comitato di amministratori indipendenti e consulenti legali esterni stia indagando significa che la questione è ormai entrata formalmente dentro la governance della società.

E per Nvidia questo pesa più che per quasi qualsiasi altra grande azienda.

Jensen Huang non è semplicemente l’amministratore delegato. Ha costruito e guidato Nvidia per più di trent’anni, è il principale interlocutore della società con governi, hyperscaler, clienti e fornitori ed è diventato una parte centrale della strategia geopolitica americana sull’AI.

Tre presidenti di commissione repubblicani della Camera gli hanno già chiesto di presentarsi al Congresso il 18 novembre per chiarire la vicenda.

Questa mattina il titolo Nvidia $NVDA ha perso oltre il 6% a Francoforte, equivalente a circa $270 miliardi di capitalizzazione rispetto alla chiusura di venerdì.

Non credo che il mercato stia prezzando oggi una sostituzione imminente di Huang.

Ma per la prima volta deve attribuire una probabilità, anche se piccola, a un rischio che fino a una settimana fa praticamente non esisteva: problemi di leadership, maggiore scrutinio sulle relazioni con la Cina o ulteriori limitazioni al business cinese.

È un rischio completamente diverso da quello che abbiamo discusso negli ultimi mesi su capex, concorrenza o valutazioni.

Ed è proprio per questo che va seguito.

Mentre il titolo Nvidia viene colpito dalla politica e dalla governance, la filiera continua a dare un messaggio opposto: memoria e packaging sono ancora troppo scarsi.

Secondo The Information, ripresa da Reuters, TSMC $TSM sta valutando per la prima volta di entrare direttamente nella produzione di memoria avanzata.

La richiesta sarebbe arrivata proprio da Nvidia $NVDA.

Il progetto riguarderebbe una nuova architettura 3D DRAM, nella quale le celle di memoria vengono impilate verticalmente per aumentare la capacità.

TSMC $TSM potrebbe costruire nuove fabbriche dedicate oppure acquistare un impianto esistente e convertirlo.

Il progetto è ancora in fase preliminare e né TSMC $TSM né Nvidia $NVDA lo hanno confermato, quindi non va trattato come una decisione definitiva.

Ma il motivo per cui viene discusso è molto più importante della singola fabbrica.

La domanda AI ha creato una scarsità abbastanza forte nella memoria da spingere il più grande produttore mondiale di chip logici a valutare l’ingresso in un mercato dominato da SK Hynix, Samsung $005930.KS e Micron $MU.

E la memoria non è l’unico vincolo.

Reuters ha ricostruito negli stessi giorni una corsa globale alla capacità di advanced packaging, la tecnologia che permette di mettere processori, memoria e altri chip nello stesso sistema ad altissima velocità.

La spesa mondiale per advanced packaging dovrebbe avvicinarsi a $28 miliardi quest’anno.

TSMC $TSM domina ancora il CoWoS, ma la capacità non è sufficiente.

Nvidia $NVDA starebbe finanziando con miliardi di dollari l’espansione della capacità CoWoS di SPIL, parte di ASE, proprio per creare più offerta fuori da TSMC $TSM.

AMD $AMD ha già annunciato oltre $10 miliardi di investimenti nella filiera taiwanese, compreso il packaging.

Questo è importante perché il collo di bottiglia dell’AI continua a spostarsi.

Prima mancavano soprattutto GPU.

Poi HBM.

Ora il problema è sempre più costruire un sistema completo nel quale GPU, memoria e networking possano essere assemblati abbastanza velocemente.

Pat Gelsinger ha stimato che in futuro il packaging avanzato potrebbe arrivare a rappresentare fino a metà del valore di un prodotto chip.

Quindi il valore economico del semiconduttore non si sta spostando soltanto verso chi disegna il processore più potente.

Si sta distribuendo anche verso chi riesce a mettere insieme decine di chip, memoria e interconnessioni in un unico sistema funzionante.

Il selloff dell’AI non ha ancora eliminato quella scarsità industriale.

Google sta finanziando direttamente un’altra alternativa a Nvidia nel data center.

Alphabet $GOOG ha rivelato di aver costruito una partecipazione da circa $548 milioni in Qualcomm $QCOM.

Qualcomm $QCOM è conosciuta soprattutto per gli smartphone, ma sta cercando di trasformarsi in un fornitore importante di processori per data center e infrastruttura AI.

E la cosa interessante è vedere chi sta sostenendo questa trasformazione.

A settembre Amazon $AMZN ha firmato un accordo che le permette di acquistare fino a $60 miliardi di chip AI per data center e altri prodotti Qualcomm $QCOM, accompagnato da warrant sulle azioni della società.

Microsoft $MSFT e Meta $META hanno già effettuato ordini per i suoi processori data center.

Ora Google $GOOG diventa anche azionista.

Qualcomm $QCOM prevede che il solo business dei chip per data center possa raggiungere $15 miliardi di ricavi entro il 2029.

Non significa che Google, Amazon, Microsoft e Meta stiano abbandonando Nvidia $NVDA.

Significa qualcosa di diverso.

I più grandi compratori di compute al mondo stanno finanziando contemporaneamente più architetture.

Producono chip internamente, comprano GPU Nvidia $NVDA e sostengono fornitori esterni alternativi.

È razionale.

Quando spendi decine di miliardi all’anno in infrastruttura, ridurre il costo per unità di compute e diminuire la dipendenza da un singolo fornitore diventa economicamente enorme.

Il mercato AI può quindi continuare a crescere rapidamente senza che ogni nuovo dollaro di capex debba necessariamente finire nella stessa architettura.

Ed è probabilmente questo il modo corretto di leggere la crescita del custom silicon.

Non necessariamente come fine del dominio Nvidia, ma come espansione di un mercato abbastanza grande da sostenere più vincitori e abbastanza importante da spingere i clienti a creare deliberatamente alternative.

I RISCHI DA TENERE D’OCCHIO

Venerdì la tecnologia ha recuperato una parte del crollo della seduta precedente.

Il Nasdaq Composite $IXIC è salito dell’1,1%, l’indice dei semiconduttori $SOXX del 4,2%, Nvidia $NVDA del 2,8% e AMD $AMD dell’11%.

Ma il Nasdaq ha comunque chiuso la quarta settimana consecutiva in ribasso, -3,4%, ed è ancora oltre il 10% sotto il massimo di ottobre.

L’S&P 500 $SPY ha perso il 2,7% nella settimana, la peggiore performance settimanale da oltre un anno.

Quindi il rimbalzo di venerdì non ha ancora cancellato il danno.

Il mercato sta cercando di capire quanto le vittorie democratiche alle elezioni di metà mandato cambieranno realmente la velocità con cui possono essere costruiti nuovi data center negli Stati Uniti.

E nel weekend Donald Trump ha aperto per la prima volta in maniera abbastanza esplicita alla possibilità di introdurre alcune protezioni sull’AI, pur ribadendo che gli Stati Uniti non possono permettersi una regolamentazione che consegni il vantaggio tecnologico alla Cina.

A questo si aggiunge il macro.

Venerdì gli Stati Uniti hanno creato 165.000 posti di lavoro in ottobre contro appena 65.000 attesi.

Il dato dei due mesi precedenti è stato inoltre rivisto complessivamente al rialzo di 84.000 posti e la disoccupazione è scesa dal 4,2% al 4,1% nonostante l’aumento della partecipazione alla forza lavoro.

Il mercato attribuisce adesso circa l’80% di probabilità a un nuovo rialzo Fed a dicembre.

Domani arriva il CPI.

Abbiamo quindi contemporaneamente tre fonti di rischio per la tecnologia: politica e regolamentazione dei data center, costo del capitale ancora elevato e, da questa mattina, un rischio specifico sulla governance della società più importante dell’intero ciclo AI.

Ma i dati provenienti da memoria, packaging e investimenti dei grandi hyperscaler continuano a raccontare una filiera nella quale la domanda fisica resta molto forte.

La distinzione tra prezzo delle azioni e domanda industriale è probabilmente la cosa più importante da seguire adesso.

THIS IS THE MOST DANGEROUS PLACE IN THE WORLD AND THE GREATEST SHOW ON EARTH.

Quantum computing's cruelest rule: reading is destroying. Measure a qubit and the superposition collapses — you get one answer, and every possibility it held dies with it. No checking your work mid-run. Every peek is demolition.

That one rule explains most of why quantum computing is hard. Classical error correction is proofreading: read the page, spot the typo, fix it. Quantum error correction has been proofreading with a blowtorch — read the page, lose the page.

Researchers now report a readout that sidesteps the rule: measure the state, keep the state. Early days, one demo rig, unreplicated. My stance on quantum headlines stays noise-until-replication.

If it holds up, though, this isn't a faster gate or a bigger qubit count. It's the load-bearing wall. Error correction goes from rebuild-blind to inspect-and-repair, and quantum memory stops being a physics in-joke. That alone would move my fault-tolerance timeline up a year — more than any qubit-count press release has ever earned.

Well damn. It's Monday, and apparently the internet has finally perfected an AI model with 100% accuracy. It's called Kick a Man While He's Down, trained on 40 trillion tokens of outrage, moral superiority and people who've never built a damn thing explaining how everyone else should live.

And today's exhibit is NVIDIA's Jensen Huang.

Look, Jensen screwed up. He admitted it, apologized to his family and colleagues, and accepted responsibility. NVIDIA's board is doing their due diligence and investigating separate national-security concerns, which absolutely deserve serious scrutiny. No one gets a free pass because they invented a GPU architecture worth several trillion dollars.

But something about our culture has become genuinely disturbing. We used to celebrate success together, criticize failures constructively, and occasionally help someone get back on their feet. Now the social contract treats another person's downfall like entertainment with 80,000 anonymous accounts examining a wardrobe malfunction.

The algorithms reward the pile-on, the spectators collect their moral superiority points, and nobody seems particularly interested in whether anything actually gets better, just goading more into their convenient outage. There's an enormous difference between demanding accountability and rooting for destruction. One builds a better world. The other just tries to buy friends, followers, impressions.

A strange way to reward a civilization.

The business and national-security story here  deserves attention. NVIDIA's board is acting responsibly. Huang says he'll cooperate.  An investigation is not a finding of guilt.  An allegation of espionage is not proof of a successful intelligence operation. 

NVIDIA earnings are next Tuesday, November 17.  So here's an uncomfortable business question. If NVIDIA has huge demand visibility, could the company withstand a leadership transition?

Conceptually, yes. A company with this much infrastructure momentum should have succession plans, an extraordinary management team, and operational systems that don't depend on a single individual. 

But nobody can seriously claim the NVIDIA ecosystem was built without Jensen's vision and execution.  Besides, the real question from an investor's perspective isn't whether the next 12 months look promising. It's whether NVIDIA can keep delivering through 2028 and beyond, when customers have more alternatives.

Now, onto the models, because the labs apparently decided to spend another weekend playing hide-and-seek. Qwen 4 is rumbling around, but not here yet. GPT-6.2 Sol has lots of chatter.  A creator claims Codex sessions using GPT-6.1 Sol may already be silently routed to a newer checkpoint. Speculation, not proof.

Beyond models, I something from my side quest! IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge National Laboratory announced a quantum error-correction co-design platform combining IBM's 120-qubit Nighthawk processor with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and EPYC CPUs. They are  connecting quantum hardware to a supercomputer.

Quantum computers make errors. Lots of them, three 9s can be a great run. To perform dependable calculations, quantum systems need to repeatedly measure error syndromes and determine how to correct the underlying information. That decoding work is classical computing, and it needs to happen quickly enough to keep pace with the quantum processor. 

The Department of Energy's 2028 target is 100 logical qubits performing 100,000 difficult operations. IBM cites experiments reaching 70 logical qubits and 438 such operations. That's approximately a 228X increase in operation count still to accomplish, along with increasing the logical-qubit count. IBM and AMD are attacking the engineering bottleneck, not merely adding more qubits to a press release.

You want more ? IBM unveiled a Quantum System Two in Chicago on Friday. Real equipment, real infrastructure, and researchers getting access to actual hardware.

Last week, we launched our gate-model quantum computing simulator beta program, marking an important milestone in D-Wave's gate-model development roadmap. Through the program, leading commercial and research organizations gain early access to D-Wave's gate-model simulator in advance of its general availability.
Participants in the simulator beta program include BBVA, a multinational financial services company based in Spain; FirstQFM, a quantum machine learning company based in Sweden; Florida Atlantic University; and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Germany.
For the first time, users will have the opportunity to experiment with error-aware programming in preparation for D-Wave's forthcoming gate-model systems.
But what is error awareness, and why does it matter for gate-model quantum computing?
 
It’s become increasingly clear that one of the greatest challenges to building practical, fault-tolerant gate-model quantum computers isn’t adding more qubits. It’s efficient error correction. At D-Wave, we believe error awareness is a critical step in overcoming that challenge.
Qubits are notoriously fragile and highly sensitive to noise. Even minor disturbances, such as electromagnetic interference or temperature fluctuations, can introduce computational errors. As quantum systems scale, these errors can accumulate and, if left uncorrected, cause the computation to fail. Effective quantum error correction is essential to scale gate-model systems capable of solving useful, real-world problems in areas such as quantum chemistry, fluid dynamics, and materials science.
In many gate-model architectures, quantum error correction requires immense amounts of quantum and classical resources, creating substantial engineering complexity, cost, and performance constraints. Emerging, resource-efficient approaches to error correction are expected to reduce this overhead dramatically, but the industry has not yet reached a scale where these approaches can be applied to near-term use cases.
D-Wave takes a different approach. With error awareness, the location of a detected error can be identified at the physical-qubit level as it occurs, allowing quantum software to adapt to those errors while the computation is still running.
We believe this unique capability, enabled by D-Wave's dual-rail qubit architecture, creates a more efficient path to quantum error correction and, ultimately, fault-tolerant gate-model quantum computers.
What Is Quantum Error Awareness and How Does It Make Error Correction More Efficient?
Quantum error awareness provides visibility into errors as they occur and the ability to respond to them during computation, reducing the resources required for error correction. Through a combination of error detection and real-time quantum-classical control, error awareness gives users new tools and data for achieving fault tolerance and exploring advanced post-noisy intermediate-scale quantum (post-NISQ) use cases.
Error awareness is made possible by the error detection capabilities of D-Wave's dual-rail architecture. In dual-rail qubits, the most common errors are photon-loss events. The hardware can detect these errors and identify the affected qubit, allowing the error to be treated as an erasure: an error with a known location. Because the error-correction system knows where the errors are, it can correct them using fewer resources than it would need for errors of unknown type and location.
Real-time quantum-classical control makes that error information actionable. Rather than waiting until the QPU has completed a run, the classical processor analyzes data while the quantum algorithm is still running and within the qubits’ coherence time. The system can then use the information to adapt subsequent quantum operations.
By combining built-in error detection and real-time control, error awareness could substantially reduce the hardware required for fault-tolerant quantum computing. We predict that, with our approach, achieving a logical error rate of 10−6, or one error in one million operations, could require only 100 to 200 physical qubits per logical qubit. This could represent up to a 10-fold reduction in physical-qubit requirements compared with conventional architectures.
Recent peer-reviewed research published in Nature validated D-Wave's dual-rail technology as a scalable foundation for commercial, fault-tolerant gate-model quantum computing. The research demonstrated a high-speed two-qubit entangling gate that achieved 99.9% fidelity when measured using error detection, while preserving the dual-rail architecture’s built-in error-detection advantages.
We believe this combination of high-fidelity qubits, hardware efficiency, and fast gate speeds provides the performance needed to support meaningful R&D, allowing researchers to move beyond theoretical models and work with real system behavior.
Build Expertise in Error-Aware Programming
D-Wave's gate-model quantum computing simulator will help developers start preparing for the era of error-aware quantum computing. We believe the simulator, built around the dual-rail architecture, is the first of its kind designed for error-aware programming. Visibility into error data will enable developers to better understand quantum behavior, develop and test error-aware algorithms and quantum error-correction techniques, and prototype post-NISQ applications today.
The simulator is accessible through D-Wave’s Leap™ quantum cloud platform and integrates with development tools, including D-Wave’s Ocean™ SDK and Qiskit. Developers can also use D-Wave’s Quantum Circuit Description Language (QCDL) API to build and run advanced error-aware quantum applications and workflows.
We plan to offer flexible development bundles that combine access to the simulator and future gate-model systems with expert guidance to streamline onboarding and support research and development. With forthcoming gate-model capabilities alongside annealing and analog-digital approaches, the platform will expand how developers can engage with quantum computing, offering hands-on exposure to multiple technologies within a single ecosystem.
We’re very excited to see the results that come out of the beta program and look forward to sharing the work that our beta customers accomplish. If you’d like to stay in the loop, sign up for updates, request future access, and be among the first to program with D-Wave's error-aware simulator:
